# The Simulated Collection {#sec-simulated-collection}

:::{.callout-note title="Draft"}
First draft, 2026-10-30. Every number in the text is computed when the book builds, and the description of each part was checked against `R/sim-collection.R` the same day. Two things are open:

- @sec-sim-agree converts a Pearson correlation to the Spearman correlation expected for normal data with $(6/\pi)\arcsin(r/2)$. It is a standard result and needs a citation.
- The parts were checked against Cook's chapter in the Cook Book [@Cook1990model]. His dissertation [@cook1985] has not been checked.
:::

Most chapters in the book try a method first on a collection I made up, where I know what went into every ring. [An Additive Model of Tree Growth](02AdditiveModel.qmd) introduces the model behind it, and [The Simulated Stand](03SimulatedStand.qmd) builds it. This appendix is the reference: how the collection is built, what each argument does, what comes back, and what is hidden in the default stand. When a chapter says "the simulated stand" and nothing more, it means the one built here with `seed = 1`.

The function is `sim.collection`. It lives in the book's `R/` folder and isn't part of `dplR`, so every chapter that uses it loads it the same way.

```{r}
#| label: a3-setup
library(dplR)
source("R/sim-collection.R")
sim <- sim.collection(seed = 1)
names(sim)
```

```{r}
#| label: a3-words
#| include: false
# spell out zero through nine in the prose
words <- function(n, cap = FALSE) {
  out <- as.character(n)
  small <- n %in% 0:9
  out[small] <- c("zero", "one", "two", "three", "four", "five", "six",
                  "seven", "eight", "nine")[n[small] + 1]
  if (cap) substr(out, 1, 1) <- toupper(substr(out, 1, 1))
  out
}
```

It returns three things. `sim$rwl` is the collection as you would have it after measuring, an `rwl` object with the years as row names and any dating errors left in. `sim$ids` says which tree and which core each series is, in the form that functions like `rwi.stats` and `treeMean` want. `sim$truth` is what you never get from a field collection: each part of every ring, separately, and a record of what was planted where. @sec-sim-returns lists it field by field.

## The Stand

```{r}
#| label: a3-stand-values
#| include: false
truthYears <- time(sim$truth$rwl)
measuredYears <- time(sim$rwl)
```

The default stand is `r sim$truth$params$n.tree` trees with `r words(sim$truth$params$n.core)` cores each, all cored in `r sim$truth$params$end.year`. Two cores from each of twenty trees is the design the Cook Book recommends for a ring-width chronology [@CookBook, p. 27]. Tree 1 is the oldest, with its pith in `r min(sim$truth$pith$pith)`, and tree `r sim$truth$params$n.tree` is the youngest, with its pith in `r max(sim$truth$pith$pith)`. The ages are spaced on a square, so old trees are few and the sample depth thins going back in time, as it does in most stands. Each core misses the pith by a few rings, a Poisson draw with a mean of five, so the two cores from one tree start in different years.

```{r}
#| label: a3-seg
#| fig-height: 7
#| fig-cap: "The default stand, one line per core from its first measured ring to the bark. Old trees are few, so the record thins going back in time."
plot(sim$rwl, plot.type = "seg")
```

The series are named for the site, a two-digit tree number and a core letter, so SIM03A is the first core from tree 3, and `autoread.ids` reads the names the same way `sim$ids` does.

One thing to watch. The tables in `sim$truth` start in `r min(truthYears)`, the year of the oldest pith, while `sim$rwl` starts in `r min(measuredYears)`, the first ring anyone measured. So the truth tables begin with `r words(min(measuredYears) - min(truthYears))` rows that have no rings in them. Some functions return `NaN` for rows like that (E.g., `pointer`), so drop them first.

## How a Ring Is Built

The parts follow Cook's aggregate model [@Cook1990model], which [chapter 2](02AdditiveModel.qmd) lays out. They are added on the log scale and exponentiated, so the spread of the widths grows with their level the way it does in wood. One ring in one core is

$$\log R_t = \log A_t + M_t + \delta D1_t + \delta D2_t, \qquad M_t = \phi M_{t-1} + C_t + T_t + E_t$$

and the measured width is $R_t$ rounded to `digits = 2`, or 0.01 mm. If a ring rounds to zero the function warns you, because `dplR` reads a zero as an absent ring. The rest of this section takes the parts one at a time.

### Age and Size, $A_t$

Each tree adds about the same basal area every year, `bai = 600` mm² in a typical tree. Trees differ in how fast they grow. Each tree's rate is drawn from a lognormal distribution with a log standard deviation of `bai.sdlog = 0.4`, independently of its age. A young tree ramps up to its rate over its first few decades, and `juv = 25` sets how quickly. The ring width is the change in radius that a year's area adds, so the rings thin as the stem grows. That is Cook's geometric argument for $A_t$ in an open stand.

In a closed canopy, Cook argued, $A_t$ has no predictable shape at all [@Cook1990model, p. 100]. So half the trees (`compete.frac = 0.5`) get a competition history on top of the geometry. It is a slow random wander: an AR(1) series with a coefficient of `compete.phi = 0.97`, smoothed with an 11-year running mean so it changes over decades, and scaled to a standard deviation of `compete = 0.3` on the log scale. Both cores of a tree share it. It counts as part of the age trend, so `sim$truth$age` includes it, and `sim$truth$competition` lists the crowded trees. Set `compete = 0` for a stand of open-grown trees.

### Climate, $C_t$

There is one climate series affecting every tree. By default it is random numbers with a little memory so that each year keeps `climate.phi = 0.3` of the year before, on top of its own new shock. You can hand the function a climate series instead, through `climate`, as a numeric vector named by year that covers every year from the oldest pith to `end.year`. The function rescales it to the size it needs and keeps its shape, and it ignores `climate.phi`. [Detrending](09Detrending.qmd) does this to give the stand slow swings in climate. `sim$truth$climate` is the series as it went into the trees, on the log scale and before the trees' memory.

### Noise, $T_t$ and $E_t$

Cook's $E_t$ is everything left over. The simulation splits it in two. $T_t$ belongs to a tree, so both of its cores carry it. $E_t$ belongs to a single core. The split is what makes two cores from one tree agree more than two trees do. Neither comes back on its own in `sim$truth`. Both are inside `memory.noise`.

### Memory, $\phi$

Climate and both kinds of noise go through an AR(1) filter that carries `phi = 0.5` of last year's value into this year. It stands in for the needles, roots and stored sugar that a good year leaves for the next one. The filter runs for 50 years before each tree's first ring, so the memory is already up to strength when the tree starts. `sim$truth$memory.noise` holds $M_t$, the filtered sum, on the log scale.

### Disturbance, $D1_t$ and $D2_t$

Both disturbances are a pulse: a jump of `size` on the log scale in one year, which then decays exponentially and falls by a factor of $e$ every `decay` years. `release` is $D1_t$ in one tree. By default tree 10 doubles its growth in 1950 (`size = log(2)`), and the boost fades over decades (`decay = 25`). `event` is $D2_t$. By default, in 1880, half the trees standing at the time (`frac = 0.5`) have their growth halved (`size = -log(2)`), and they recover over a decade or so (`decay = 8`). Which trees it hits is drawn at random, and `sim$truth$event$trees` lists them by number.

Cook defines $D2_t$ by its turning up in every tree [@Cook1990model, p. 102]. Hitting half the stand keeps the event visible as something other than climate, which is what chapter 2 needs. `frac = 1` gives Cook's version.

The disturbances are added after the memory filter, so each one keeps its shape. Cook treats disturbance as a shock that passes through a tree's memory the way climate does [@CookBook, p. 130], and the simulation doesn't. `sim$truth$disturbance` holds $D1_t + D2_t$ for each core, on the log scale.

### Dating Errors

Errors go in last, and only into `sim$rwl`. `sim$truth$rwl` keeps the widths as the trees grew them. `errors` is a data frame with three columns: the series, the true calendar year of the ring, and the type. A `"missing"` ring is deleted, and every ring inside it is labeled a year too late. A `"false"` ring splits one ring into two, at 40% and 60% of its width, and every ring inside it is labeled a year too early. A series can take more than one error. The default deletes the `r sim$truth$errors$year` ring from `r sim$truth$errors$series`.

## Setting How Well the Trees Agree {#sec-sim-agree}

You don't set the size of each part directly. You set how well the cores agree, and the function works out the sizes. Three arguments do it.

- `sd.hf = 0.25` is the standard deviation of $M_t$ on the log scale, the year-to-year part of growth.
- `rbar.bt = 0.4` is the share of that variance that comes from climate. It is the correlation you would expect between two trees.
- `rbar.wt = 0.6` is the share that comes from climate and tree noise together. It is the correlation you would expect between two cores of one tree.

Core noise gets the rest. When the climate has memory, all three parts are shrunk by one common factor, so $M_t$ keeps the standard deviation you asked for and the shares stay where you set them.

The targets apply to the year-to-year part with the memory taken out. So they are what you would expect from prewhitened indices if detrending were perfect. The truth lets you try that: `exp(sim$truth$memory.noise)` is each core with its age trend and its disturbances divided out exactly.

```{r}
#| label: a3-agree
# Each core with its age trend and disturbances removed exactly, labeled as
# indices so that rwi.stats accepts it
perfect <- as.rwi(exp(sim$truth$memory.noise))

# rbar with rwi.stats' default, Spearman's rank correlation, and then with
# Pearson's
spearmanStats <- rwi.stats(perfect, sim$ids, prewhiten = TRUE)
pearsonStats <- rwi.stats(perfect, sim$ids, prewhiten = TRUE,
                          method = "pearson")
rbind(spearman = spearmanStats[, c("rbar.wt", "rbar.bt")],
      pearson = pearsonStats[, c("rbar.wt", "rbar.bt")])
```

```{r}
#| label: a3-agree-many
#| include: false
# The same check on twenty stands, for the averages in the text. The last
# two numbers skip rwi.stats: on the log scale, with white climate so there
# is only the tree's memory to undo, they take out that memory with the
# true phi and correlate what is left.
manyStats <- sapply(1:20, function(s) {
  stand <- sim.collection(seed = s, release = NULL, event = NULL,
                          errors = NULL)
  idx <- as.rwi(exp(stand$truth$memory.noise))
  sp <- rwi.stats(idx, stand$ids, prewhiten = TRUE)
  pe <- rwi.stats(idx, stand$ids, prewhiten = TRUE, method = "pearson")
  white <- sim.collection(seed = s, release = NULL, event = NULL,
                          errors = NULL, climate.phi = 0)
  m <- as.matrix(white$truth$memory.noise)
  shocks <- m[-1, ] - white$truth$params$phi * m[-nrow(m), ]
  r <- cor(shocks, use = "pairwise.complete.obs")
  same <- outer(white$ids$tree, white$ids$tree, "==")
  up <- upper.tri(r)
  c(sp.wt = sp$rbar.wt, sp.bt = sp$rbar.bt,
    pe.wt = pe$rbar.wt, pe.bt = pe$rbar.bt,
    sh.wt = mean(r[same & up]), sh.bt = mean(r[!same & up]))
})
manyMeans <- round(rowMeans(manyStats), 3)
# Spearman's correlation expected for normal data with Pearson correlation r
spearmanOf <- function(r) round(6 / pi * asin(r / 2), 3)
```

At seed 1 they are at `r sprintf("%.3f", spearmanStats$rbar.wt)` and `r sprintf("%.3f", spearmanStats$rbar.bt)` with `rwi.stats` as it comes, and at `r sprintf("%.3f", pearsonStats$rbar.wt)` and `r sprintf("%.3f", pearsonStats$rbar.bt)` with Pearson's correlation, against targets of `r sim$truth$params$rbar.wt` and `r sim$truth$params$rbar.bt`. One stand is one draw, so here are twenty, built with seeds 1 to 20. Go straight to what was built, on the log scale with the true memory divided out (and with white climate, so there is only one memory to undo), and they average `r sprintf("%.3f", manyMeans["sh.wt"])` and `r sprintf("%.3f", manyMeans["sh.bt"])`. So the stands are built to their targets. Two things take the numbers down from there.

The first is that `rwi.stats` works on indices and has to fit its own AR model. The parts are built on the log scale and the indices are their exponentials, and prewhitening fits an AR model to each core where the simulation knows the true one. With Pearson's correlation, the twenty stands average `r sprintf("%.3f", manyMeans["pe.wt"])` and `r sprintf("%.3f", manyMeans["pe.bt"])`.

The second is the kind of correlation. `rwi.stats` uses Spearman's rank correlation unless you ask for another, and on normally distributed data Spearman's runs a little under Pearson's. The targets are Pearson correlations, and a Pearson correlation of `r sim$truth$params$rbar.wt` or `r sim$truth$params$rbar.bt` comes out at about `r spearmanOf(sim$truth$params$rbar.wt)` or `r spearmanOf(sim$truth$params$rbar.bt)` as Spearman's. With the default, the twenty stands average `r sprintf("%.3f", manyMeans["sp.wt"])` and `r sprintf("%.3f", manyMeans["sp.bt"])`.

So `rwi.stats` reports a few hundredths under the targets before any method has touched the rings, with each of the two steps taking about half. Keep that in mind when you compare a statistic from the simulation with the value it was built with.

## The Default Stand

Here is what is planted in the stand built with `seed = 1`, tree by tree. Chapters that use the stand point back to this table.

```{r}
#| label: a3-default
truth <- sim$truth
trees <- truth$pith
treeNumber <- seq_len(nrow(trees))

# truth$competition names the crowded trees ("SIM02", ...), while the event
# and the release give tree numbers
trees$crowded <- trees$tree %in% truth$competition
trees$event <- treeNumber %in% truth$event$trees
trees$release <- treeNumber == truth$release$tree

# sim$ids turns each planted error's series into its tree number. match()
# finds which error, if any, belongs to each tree.
errorTree <- sim$ids[truth$errors$series, "tree"]
errorRow <- match(treeNumber, errorTree)
trees$error <- ifelse(is.na(errorRow), "",
                      paste(truth$errors$series[errorRow],
                            truth$errors$type[errorRow],
                            truth$errors$year[errorRow]))
trees
```

```{r}
#| label: a3-default-values
#| include: false
nStanding <- sum(truth$pith$pith < truth$event$year)
nHit <- length(truth$event$trees)
errTree <- errorTree[1]
errNotes <- c("crowded"[trees$crowded[errTree]],
              "hit by the event"[trees$event[errTree]])
```

Of the `r nrow(trees)` trees, `r words(length(truth$competition))` are crowded. The `r truth$event$year` event hits `r words(nHit)` of the `r nStanding` trees whose pith is older than the event. The release is in tree `r truth$release$tree`. Tree `r errTree`, the one with the missing ring, is also `r paste(errNotes, collapse = " and ")`, which is worth remembering when `r truth$errors$series[1]` looks odd in more than one way.

## What Comes Back {#sec-sim-returns}

| Field | What it holds |
|---|---|
| `rwl` | The widths as measured, with any dating errors, from the first measured ring. Class `rwl`. |
| `ids` | The tree and core number of each series. |
| `truth$rwl` | The widths as the trees grew them, before any dating errors, from the oldest pith. Class `rwl`. |
| `truth$age` | $A_t$ for each core in mm, competition included. |
| `truth$memory.noise` | $M_t$ for each core: climate and noise after the tree's memory, on the log scale. |
| `truth$disturbance` | $D1_t + D2_t$ for each core, on the log scale. |
| `truth$climate` | A data frame of year and $C_t$, the climate as it went into the trees, on the log scale. |
| `truth$release` | The release as given: tree, year, size and decay. |
| `truth$event` | The event as given, plus `trees`, the numbers of the trees it hit. |
| `truth$errors` | The dating errors as given. |
| `truth$pith` | Each tree's name and pith year. |
| `truth$competition` | The names of the crowded trees. |
| `truth$params` | The other arguments, as used, including the seed. |

The parts multiply back into the widths. `truth$age * exp(truth$memory.noise + truth$disturbance)`, rounded to 0.01 mm, is `truth$rwl`.

## Arguments

| Argument | Default | What it does |
|---|---|---|
| `n.tree` | `20` | Number of trees. |
| `n.core` | `2` | Cores per tree, up to 26. |
| `end.year` | `2025` | The year every tree is cored, and the outside ring of every core. |
| `age.range` | `c(120, 380)` | Ages of the youngest and oldest trees. |
| `rbar.bt` | `0.4` | Target correlation between trees, the climate's share of $M_t$. |
| `rbar.wt` | `0.6` | Target correlation between cores of one tree, the share of climate and tree noise. |
| `sd.hf` | `0.25` | Standard deviation of $M_t$ on the log scale. |
| `phi` | `0.5` | The tree's memory, the AR(1) coefficient on climate and noise. |
| `climate` | `NULL` | A climate series named by year. `NULL` draws one. |
| `climate.phi` | `0.3` | Memory in the drawn climate. Ignored when you pass `climate`. |
| `bai` | `600` | Basal area added each year by a typical tree, in mm². |
| `bai.sdlog` | `0.4` | How much growth rates vary from tree to tree. |
| `juv` | `25` | How quickly a young tree ramps up to its growth rate, in years. |
| `compete` | `0.3` | Size of the competition wander on the log scale. `0` turns it off. |
| `compete.frac` | `0.5` | Share of the trees that are crowded. |
| `compete.phi` | `0.97` | How slowly the competition wander moves. |
| `pith.miss` | `5` | Mean number of rings by which a core misses the pith. |
| `release` | `list(tree = 10, year = 1950, size = log(2), decay = 25)` | $D1_t$ in one tree. `NULL` turns it off. |
| `event` | `list(year = 1880, frac = 0.5, size = -log(2), decay = 8)` | $D2_t$ across the stand. `NULL` turns it off. |
| `errors` | `data.frame(series = "SIM03A", year = 1800, type = "missing")` | Dating errors to plant. `NULL` plants none. |
| `site` | `"SIM"` | The site code at the start of each series name. |
| `digits` | `2` | Decimal places the widths are rounded to. |
| `seed` | `NULL` | A random seed. `NULL` gives a different stand every time. |

## Making Your Own

Change the arguments and you get a different stand. A few that the book uses:

```{r}
#| label: a3-variants
#| eval: false
# A clean stand: no release, no event and no dating errors
clean <- sim.collection(seed = 1, release = NULL, event = NULL, errors = NULL)

# A weak stand, where the trees agree about half as well
weak <- sim.collection(seed = 1, rbar.bt = 0.2, rbar.wt = 0.4)

# Open-grown trees only, under climate with no memory
open <- sim.collection(seed = 1, compete = 0, climate.phi = 0)

# Two missing rings in one core and a false ring in another
errs <- data.frame(series = c("SIM03A", "SIM03A", "SIM07B"),
                   year = c(1800, 1900, 1850),
                   type = c("missing", "missing", "false"))
messy <- sim.collection(seed = 1, errors = errs)
```

The seed fixes every random draw, so the same call gives the same stand every time. Arguments that only set a size, like `rbar.bt`, `sd.hf`, `compete` or `climate.phi`, scale the same draws, so `weak` is the default stand with its agreement turned down. Arguments that change what gets drawn shift every draw after them. Turning the event off keeps the climate and the noise but picks different crowded trees, and passing your own climate gives you different trees altogether.

## What It Leaves Out

[The Simulated Stand](03SimulatedStand.qmd) sets the stand beside Hurricane Ridge and lists what field collections have that the simulation doesn't. A few of the simplifications favor particular methods, so keep them in mind when a method does better here than you expected.

- Every open-grown tree has the same shape of age trend, scaled by its growth rate. That suits a regional curve unusually well.
- A tree's growth rate has nothing to do with its age. In the field, trees that grow slowly tend to live longer, and that biases a regional curve. [Regional Curves](12RegionalCurves.qmd) adds the link to show what it does.
- Every tree is cored in the same year, so the stand is all living trees. [Regional Curves](12RegionalCurves.qmd) joins stands that end in different centuries to get past that.
- Rings go missing only where you plant the errors. A narrow ring always forms all the way around.
- The only measurement error is the rounding.
- There is one climate, the same in every tree, with no swing slower than its own memory unless you pass one in.
